 SpaceX’s latest quarter rides AI surge and Starlink growth 
 SpaceX reported a sharp jump in quarterly profit as revenue surged 161 per cent, with its Super Intelligence business emerging as the biggest growth driver. Starlink also delivered strong gains, while heavy capital spending on computing infrastructure signalled that the company is betting big on AI as well as space. ETRajasthan

 SpaceX ’s latest quarterly numbers show how quickly the company’s mix of businesses is changing. According to Times of India , the aerospace group posted a net profit of $4.4 billion in the July-September quarter, powered less by rockets alone and more by a fast-expanding artificial intelligence and computing arm. Revenue climbed 161 per cent year on year to $14.6 billion, while adjusted EBITDA rose 306 per cent to $8.8 billion. The result marked a sharp reversal from the same quarter a year earlier, when the company reported a net loss of $1.1 billion on revenue of $5.6 billion. The figures also point to a business that is scaling aggressively, even as capital spending accelerates in parallel. AI and computing emerge as the main growth engine The biggest shift in the quarter came from SpaceX ’s Super Intelligence business, which covers computing infrastructure, models and software applications. That division generated $7.6 billion in revenue, up 830 per cent from $813 million a year earlier. The segment added $6.7 billion in year-on-year revenue through solutions and infrastructure, helped by new cloud services agreements, the acquisition of Cursor and broader adoption of Grok products by enterprise customers and consumers, the report said. This marks a notable evolution for a company long associated with launch services and satellite broadband. The numbers suggest that computing capacity and software monetisation are now sitting alongside space launch operations as core contributors to growth. For investors, that changes the profile of the business: it is no longer only a capital-intensive aerospace story, but also a high-growth technology platform with recurring demand from enterprise and consumer users. Starlink continues to carry scale and cash flow Connectivity remained the other major pillar of the quarter. Starlink brought in $5.2 billion in revenue, up 69 per cent from $3.1 billion a year earlier, while operating income rose 99 per cent to $2.4 billion. The consumer subscriber base reached 13.6 million as of September 30, compared with 7.2 million a year earlier, and the network added 1.6 million users during the quarter. Average monthly revenue per user increased to $69 from $66 in the previous quarter, indicating that growth was not driven solely by volume. That matters because Starlink has become one of the clearest examples of how satellite connectivity can move from a niche service to a broad consumer and enterprise product. For SpaceX, the segment provides a steadier revenue stream than launch work and helps support the heavy investment cycle elsewhere in the business. Launches, Starship and the space business still matter Traditional space operations continued to contribute meaningfully, even if they were no longer the headline driver. Space-related activities generated $1.8 billion in revenue, up 6 per cent from a year earlier, and the company completed 12 customer launches in the quarter. The report also noted that the first orbital Starship flight deployed 26 Starlink V3 satellites, a milestone that added roughly 10 times the downlink capacity of a Falcon 9 Starlink launch. That detail is important because it links the rocket programme directly to the satellite broadband business. In practical terms, the larger Starship payload capacity could reduce launch costs per satellite and improve the economics of network expansion. For a company trying to scale both hardware and services, that combination is strategically significant. Heavy investment is reshaping the balance sheet The growth story came with a steep rise in spending. Capital expenditure reached $19.6 billion in the third quarter, compared with $6.9 billion in the same period last year, largely because of investment in computing infrastructure. Computing capacity stood at 1.7 gigawatts by September 30, up from 0.6 gigawatts a year earlier, as the company continued to build out the backbone for its Super Intelligence business. That level of outlay suggests the company is entering a phase where infrastructure buildout is as important as revenue growth. The challenge now is not whether demand exists, but whether the company can convert rapid expansion into durable returns without overextending its balance sheet. The CFO said the company aims to keep scaling while maintaining discipline, stressing capital efficiency, strong returns on invested capital and a robust investment-grade balance sheet. For now, the latest quarter shows a company pulling together three powerful growth engines: AI infrastructure, satellite internet and launch services. The mix is unusual, but it has given SpaceX a much broader financial base than a pure launch provider would have. If the company can keep monetising computing capacity while Starlink’s subscriber base expands and Starship improves launch economics, the next phase of growth could look very different from its past.
